title: The dual write and the transactional outbox
summary: Why "save, then publish" loses events, and how an outbox table in the same transaction fixes it.

steps.title: The dual write
body: `orders-api` saves an order and tells the world about it:
```csharp fragment
db.Orders.Add(order);
await db.SaveChangesAsync();                                  // write 1: the database
await producer.ProduceAsync("orders", new Message<string, string> { Key = order.Id, Value = json });  // write 2: the broker
Two systems, two writes, no transaction spanning both. Every way it can go wrong does, at scale:
| What fails | Result |
| Broker down or the pod dies after `SaveChangesAsync` | order exists, **no event**: nobody ships it |
| Publish first, then the database write fails | **ghost event**: shipping ships an order that does not exist |
| Two requests interleave | events can reach the broker in a different order than the commits |
Distributed transactions (XA / 2PC) are not the answer: Kafka and RabbitMQ do not take part in them, and where
they exist they couple your uptime to every participant. The fix is to make it **one** write.

steps.prompt: `orders-api` saves the order, then publishes `OrderPlaced`. The broker is unreachable for 30 seconds; the code logs the exception and still returns `201 Created`. What is the state afterwards?
options: The orders exist in the database but no events were published, so downstream services never hear about them
The orders were rolled back automatically
The broker client buffered the events and will deliver them
Nothing is wrong: the events will be republished on the next request
explain: The database transaction committed before the publish was attempted. Some clients buffer briefly (librdkafka keeps
messages in memory until `message.timeout.ms`), but a pod restart loses that buffer too. "Log and carry on" turns a
broker blip into silent data loss.

steps.title: The transactional outbox
body: Write the event into an **outbox table in the same database transaction** as the business change. A separate
**relay** publishes outbox rows later and marks them sent.
```text
orders-api                          one DB transaction
├─ INSERT INTO orders ...          ┐
└─ INSERT INTO outbox (id, type,   ┘ both or neither
aggregate_id, payload)
relay (loop)                         broker
SELECT unpublished ORDER BY id ──► publish (wait for confirm / acks=all)
UPDATE outbox SET published_at ◄── confirmed
```sql
SELECT id, type, aggregate_id, payload
FROM outbox
WHERE published_at IS NULL
ORDER BY id
LIMIT 100
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;         -- PostgreSQL / MySQL 8; SQL Server: WITH (UPDLOCK, READPAST)
- **Polling relay**: simple, costs a query every interval and adds up to one interval of latency.
- **CDC relay**: a tool such as Debezium reads the database log (PostgreSQL WAL, MySQL binlog) and publishes
outbox inserts; low latency, no polling, but one more system to run.
- The relay is **at-least-once**: it can crash after publishing and before marking the row. Publish with the
outbox `id` as the message id so consumers can dedup.
- **Ordering**: publish in `id` order and stop at the first failure, or a later event for the same order overtakes
an earlier one. Use the aggregate id (order id) as the Kafka key so per-order order survives partitioning.
- **Cleanup**: delete published rows older than a few days, or the table grows forever.

steps.prompt: Put one iteration of the polling relay in order.
lines: Read up to 100 unpublished rows ordered by id (FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED)
Publish each row's payload with the outbox id as the message id
Wait for the broker to confirm (publisher confirm / acks=all)
Set published_at on the confirmed rows and commit
If the batch was empty, sleep briefly before the next iteration
explain: Marking a row as published before the broker confirmed it brings the lost-event bug back. Marking it after means a
crash in between republishes it: a duplicate, which the message id makes harmless.

steps.prompt: The relay crashes after publishing row 1 but before marking it. Then it restarts and runs normally. What does this print?
code: var outbox = new List<(int Id, string Payload, bool Published)> { (1, "o-1", false), (2, "o-2", false) };
explain: Row 1 is published twice, with the same id both times. The outbox turns "maybe lost" into "maybe duplicated", and
the consumer's inbox (next lesson) turns "maybe duplicated" into "processed once".

steps.prompt: Complete the relay's query so several relay instances can run without blocking each other or publishing the same rows.
explain: `SKIP LOCKED` makes a second relay take the next unlocked rows instead of waiting. `NOWAIT` would make it fail
immediately instead. Ordering by `id` (a sequence) is the commit order you want to preserve; `created_at` can tie.

steps.prompt: Match each outbox design choice to why you would make it.
pairs: Polling relay
Simplest to run; latency is the poll interval
CDC relay (Debezium on the WAL / binlog)
Low latency without polling queries, at the cost of another system
`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`
Several relay instances take different rows without blocking
Outbox id as the message id
Consumers can drop a republished copy
Delete rows published more than 7 days ago
Keeps the outbox table and its index small
explain: All five show up in a real outbox review. The one teams forget is cleanup: an outbox with 400 million rows makes
the relay's query slow, and the relay lag climbs.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: finding lost and duplicate messages
steps.body: Reach for these when someone reports a message that never arrived or arrived twice, and when you replay after a fix.

toolkit.cmd: kafka-console-consumer.sh --bootstrap-server kafka:9092 --topic payments-charged --from-beginning --formatter-property print.key=true --formatter-property print.partition=true --formatter-property print.offset=true --formatter-property print.headers=true
toolkit.what: Kafka: read the topic with keys, partitions, offsets and headers.
flags: start at the oldest retained record
toolkit.when: The same key or message-id header at two offsets is a duplicate; a missing one is a loss.

toolkit.what: Where the group stands on every partition.
flags: what a restart resumes from; everything after it will be delivered again

toolkit.when: The group must have no active members, and the handler must be idempotent.

toolkit.cmd: rabbitmqctl list_queues name messages_ready messages_unacknowledged consumers
toolkit.what: RabbitMQ: what is waiting and what is in flight.
flags: work in flight: if that consumer dies, all of it is redelivered
they go back marked redelivered, so never on a busy production queue

toolkit.cmd: SELECT count(*), min(created_at) FROM outbox WHERE published_at IS NULL;
toolkit.when: Alert when the oldest unpublished row is older than a minute.

toolkit.cmd: new ProducerConfig { Acks = Acks.All, EnableIdempotence = true, MaxInFlight = 5 }
toolkit.what: A Kafka producer that does not lose or duplicate.
flags: no duplicates on retry (not the default in Confluent.Kafka)
5 or less keeps ordering with idempotence

toolkit.cmd: new ConsumerConfig { EnableAutoOffsetStore = false, IsolationLevel = IsolationLevel.ReadCommitted }
toolkit.what: A Kafka consumer that commits only finished work.

toolkit.cmd: await channel.BasicConsumeAsync(queue: "billing", autoAck: false, consumer: consumer);
toolkit.what: RabbitMQ: ack after the work, not on delivery.
flags: the message stays unacked until you BasicAckAsync it

toolkit.what: RabbitMQ: publish from the outbox with confirms and a stable id.
flags: set from the outbox id, so consumers can spot duplicates
the channel to publish on: the relay marks a row only after the confirm

steps.prompt: Match each reading to what it tells you.
pairs: The same message-id header at two offsets
A duplicate
A message-id that never appears on the topic
A loss
`ack_required false` in `list_consumers`
autoAck: at-most-once delivery
A large `messages_unacknowledged`
Work that is redelivered if the consumer dies
`CURRENT-OFFSET` in `--describe`
Where a restart resumes; later records arrive again

steps.prompt: Configure the payments producer so it neither loses nor duplicates and keeps per-partition order.
steps.explain: `Acks.All` waits for the in-sync replicas, idempotence stops duplicates on retry and is not on by default in Confluent.Kafka, and up to 5 requests in flight keep ordering with idempotence.

steps.title: Fix the dual write
prompt: **Symptom.** Shipping found 212 orders from last night with no `OrderPlaced` event. The API log at that time:
```text
02:14:09 ERR orders-api PlaceOrder o-5521 saved, publish failed:
BrokerUnreachableException: None of the specified endpoints were reachable
`PlaceOrder` saves the order, commits, then publishes directly. Change it to the **transactional outbox**: add the
event to the same transaction as the order, and do not publish from the request at all (a relay does that). Keep
the signature; `broker` becomes unused.
The tests give you these types (already defined):
```csharp
class Tx       { List<string> Orders; List<(string Type, string Payload)> Outbox; }
class Database { Tx Begin(); void Commit(Tx tx);   // all or nothing; throws InvalidOperationException on a failed commit
List<string> Orders; List<OutboxRow> Outbox; }   // OutboxRow(long Id, string Type, string Payload)
class Broker   { void Publish(string type, string payload); }    // throws while the broker is down
The event type is `"OrderPlaced"` and its payload is the order id.
starter: void PlaceOrder(Database db, Broker broker, string orderId)
solution: void PlaceOrder(Database db, Broker broker, string orderId)
hints: `Tx` has an `Outbox` list next to `Orders`. What belongs there?
Add `("OrderPlaced", orderId)` to `tx.Outbox` before `db.Commit(tx)`, and delete the `broker.Publish` line.
template: {{CODE}}
var dojoDb = new Database();
var dojoBroker = new Broker { Down = true };
var dojoThrew = false;
try { PlaceOrder(dojoDb, dojoBroker, "o-1"); } catch { dojoThrew = true; }
Dojo.Check("broker down: PlaceOrder still succeeds", !dojoThrew, "PlaceOrder threw while the broker was down");
Dojo.Eq("the order is saved", new List<string> { "o-1" }, dojoDb.Orders);
Dojo.Eq("the event waits in the outbox", new List<string> { "OrderPlaced:o-1" }, dojoDb.Outbox.Select(r => r.Type + ":" + r.Payload).ToList());
Dojo.Eq("nothing is published from the request", 0, dojoBroker.Sent.Count);
dojoDb.FailNextCommit = true;
Dojo.Throws<InvalidOperationException>("a failed commit is reported to the caller", () => PlaceOrder(dojoDb, dojoBroker, "o-2"));
Dojo.Check("a failed commit leaves neither the order nor the event", !dojoDb.Orders.Contains("o-2") && dojoDb.Outbox.All(r => r.Payload != "o-2"), "found o-2 in Orders or Outbox");
dojoBroker.Down = false;
PlaceOrder(dojoDb, dojoBroker, "o-3");
Dojo.Eq("outbox ids follow commit order", new List<long> { 1, 2 }, dojoDb.Outbox.Select(r => r.Id).ToList());
class Tx
public List<string> Orders { get; } = new();
public List<(string Type, string Payload)> Outbox { get; } = new();
record OutboxRow(long Id, string Type, string Payload);
class Database
public List<string> Orders { get; } = new();
public List<OutboxRow> Outbox { get; } = new();
public bool FailNextCommit { get; set; }
long dojoNextId = 1;
public Tx Begin() => new Tx();
public void Commit(Tx tx)
if (FailNextCommit) { FailNextCommit = false; throw new InvalidOperationException("deadlock victim: transaction rolled back"); }
Orders.AddRange(tx.Orders);
foreach (var (type, payload) in tx.Outbox) Outbox.Add(new OutboxRow(dojoNextId++, type, payload));
class Broker
public bool Down { get; set; }
public List<string> Sent { get; } = new();
public void Publish(string type, string payload)
if (Down) throw new InvalidOperationException("BrokerUnreachableException: None of the specified endpoints were reachable");
Sent.Add(type + ":" + payload);

forbid.message: Does not publish from inside the request

steps.title: Build the outbox relay
prompt: Now the relay. Write a class `OutboxRelay`:
- `OutboxRelay(List<OutboxMessage> table, Func<OutboxMessage, bool> publish)`: `publish` returns `true` when the
broker **confirmed** the message, `false` when it failed.
- `int RunOnce(int batchSize, long now)`: take the unpublished rows (`PublishedAt == null`) in `Id` order, at most
`batchSize`; publish them one by one; set `PublishedAt = now` on each confirmed row. On the **first** failure stop
the batch (a later event for the same order must not overtake it). Return how many were published.
- `int Cleanup(long now, long keepMinutes)`: delete rows published `keepMinutes` or more ago
(`now - PublishedAt >= keepMinutes`). Never delete an unpublished row. Return how many were deleted.
`OutboxMessage` is defined by the tests (times are minutes):
```csharp
class OutboxMessage
public long Id { get; init; }
public string AggregateId { get; init; }
public string Payload { get; init; }
public long CreatedAt { get; init; }
public long? PublishedAt { get; set; }   // null = not published yet
starter: public OutboxRelay(List<OutboxMessage> table, Func<OutboxMessage, bool> publish)
public int RunOnce(int batchSize, long now) => 0;
public int Cleanup(long now, long keepMinutes) => 0;
solution: public OutboxRelay(List<OutboxMessage> table, Func<OutboxMessage, bool> publish)
public int RunOnce(int batchSize, long now)
var batch = table.Where(m => m.PublishedAt == null).OrderBy(m => m.Id).Take(batchSize).ToList();
if (!publish(m)) break;      // keep order: never skip past a failed row
m.PublishedAt = now;         // only after the broker confirmed
public int Cleanup(long now, long keepMinutes) =>
table.RemoveAll(m => m.PublishedAt is long at && now - at >= keepMinutes);
hints: In the loop: `if (!publish(m)) break;` then stamp the row and count it.
`table.RemoveAll(m => m.PublishedAt is long at && now - at >= keepMinutes)` returns the number removed.
template: var dojoTable = new List<OutboxMessage>
new() { Id = 3, AggregateId = "o-2", Payload = "OrderPlaced o-2", CreatedAt = 1 },
new() { Id = 1, AggregateId = "o-1", Payload = "OrderPlaced o-1", CreatedAt = 0 },
new() { Id = 2, AggregateId = "o-1", Payload = "OrderPaid o-1", CreatedAt = 0 },
new() { Id = 4, AggregateId = "o-1", Payload = "OrderShipped o-1", CreatedAt = 2 },
var dojoSent = new List<string>();
var dojoFailOn = "";
var dojoRelay = new OutboxRelay(dojoTable, m => { if (m.Payload == dojoFailOn) return false; dojoSent.Add(m.Payload); return true; });
Dojo.Eq("a batch of 2 publishes the two oldest rows", 2, dojoRelay.RunOnce(2, 10));
Dojo.Eq("rows go out in id order", new List<string> { "OrderPlaced o-1", "OrderPaid o-1" }, dojoSent);
Dojo.Eq("published rows are stamped with the time", 10L, dojoTable.Single(m => m.Id == 1).PublishedAt ?? -1L);
dojoFailOn = "OrderPlaced o-2";
Dojo.Eq("a failed publish stops the batch", 0, dojoRelay.RunOnce(10, 11));
Dojo.Check("o-1's OrderShipped did not overtake the failed row", !dojoSent.Contains("OrderShipped o-1"), "row 4 was published while row 3 was failing");
Dojo.Check("the failed row stays unpublished", dojoTable.Single(m => m.Id == 3).PublishedAt == null, "row 3 was marked published");
dojoFailOn = "";
Dojo.Eq("the next run catches up", 2, dojoRelay.RunOnce(10, 12));
Dojo.Eq("everything in order", new List<string> { "OrderPlaced o-1", "OrderPaid o-1", "OrderPlaced o-2", "OrderShipped o-1" }, dojoSent);
Dojo.Eq("nothing left to publish", 0, dojoRelay.RunOnce(10, 13));
Dojo.Eq("cleanup keeps rows published less than 60 minutes ago", 0, dojoRelay.Cleanup(69, 60));
Dojo.Eq("cleanup removes rows published 60 minutes ago", 2, dojoRelay.Cleanup(70, 60));
Dojo.Eq("rows left", new List<long> { 3, 4 }, dojoTable.Select(m => m.Id).OrderBy(x => x).ToList());
dojoTable.Add(new OutboxMessage { Id = 5, AggregateId = "o-3", Payload = "OrderPlaced o-3", CreatedAt = 0 });
Dojo.Eq("cleanup removes the old published rows only", 2, dojoRelay.Cleanup(1000, 60));
Dojo.Eq("the unpublished row survives cleanup", new List<long> { 5 }, dojoTable.Select(m => m.Id).ToList());
{{CODE}}
class OutboxMessage
public long Id { get; init; }
public string AggregateId { get; init; } = "";
public string Payload { get; init; } = "";
public long CreatedAt { get; init; }
public long? PublishedAt { get; set; }
